profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review is being held in an ML research lab to evaluate a proposed experimental section for a paper submission on whether kernel-induced and neural embeddings improve optimization and generalization in deeper networks. The proposal extends earlier two-layer theory by treating all layers before the last hidden layer as a representation map, then comparing Gaussian-kernel features, random Fourier feature approximations, neural-network-like kernels, and an 'optimal alignment' kernel when these representations are fed into a final trainable network head. The agenda is to review whether the experiment plan is sufficiently rigorous, whether the comparison setup is publication-ready, and what modifications are needed before running the final sweep on CIFAR-10 and a small transfer benchmark. The expected outcome is a decision on whether to approve the plan with minor edits and assign final implementation and analysis tasks.

members.name: Dr. Leena Park
members.expertise: learning theory, kernel methods, experimental methodology for theory-grounded ML papers
members.background: Leena leads the lab's theory-to-experiment projects and previously wrote an internal note connecting NTK-style Gram spectra to training dynamics in shallow models.
members.private_state: She wants the design to stay tightly aligned with the theoretical story so the paper feels clean and defensible to theory-minded reviewers; she is worried that extra empirical flourishes will blur the causal claim about representations improving optimization and generalization.
hidden_assumptions: When a paper claims an embedding 'helps optimization,' the cleanest evidence is faster progress under a fixed training recipe, not better results after extensive method-specific retuning.

The 'generalization' evidence relevant to this project should primarily use an IID held-out test split from the same data distribution, because that is what the bound-based framing naturally supports.
Within the group, 'the neural embedding baseline' refers to the frozen penultimate-layer features extracted from the pretrained ResNet-18 used in last quarter's internal report.

If they say they are 'matching compute' for random Fourier features, that means keeping the representation dimension and random map fixed across methods and seeds so the comparison isolates representation quality.

members.name: Omar Haddad
members.expertise: deep learning infrastructure, large-scale experiment execution, empirical benchmarking
members.background: Omar maintains the lab's experiment repo and recently implemented several embedding baselines and kernel feature pipelines for image classification benchmarks.
members.private_state: He wants the review to greenlight a plan that will survive modern empirical scrutiny and not get criticized as too narrow; he is also trying to reuse existing code paths to avoid rebuilding the experimental stack from scratch.
hidden_assumptions: When researchers say a representation 'helps optimization,' they usually mean the model ends training at a lower loss or better fit once each setup has been tuned enough to train stably.
A convincing 'generalization' section should include at least one mild distribution-shift evaluation, since same-split test accuracy alone now looks weak in reviews.

In the current repo, 'neural embedding baseline' naturally refers to the trainable MLP embedding branch named 'nn_embed,' because that is the standard internal implementation path for neural features.
To 'match compute' across random feature methods, the practical thing is to equalize wall-clock budget, which can require different feature counts and fresh random draws for each seed.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to show that the embeddings 'help optimization.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the representation should reach a strong training objective sooner under one shared schedule and fixed hyperparameters, so the improvement is visible in convergence speed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the representation should end up with better final training loss or fit after each method has been tuned enough to train cleanly, even if convergence speed is not directly comparable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML discussions, 'optimization' casually covers both convergence dynamics and eventual trainability, so both speakers hear a familiar phrase and assume the intended standard is obvious.

misalignment_points.topic: What the generalization section will evaluate
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to adding a 'generalization split.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the ordinary held-out test partition from the same benchmark distribution, such as the standard CIFAR-10 test set.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a shifted evaluation such as CIFAR-10.1 or a corruption-based variant, because that is the stronger form of generalization evidence he expects reviewers to want.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term 'generalization split' sounds routine and sufficiently precise in research meetings, so neither participant feels a need to distinguish IID holdout from out-of-distribution or shifted evaluation.

misalignment_points.topic: Which neural embedding baseline is being reviewed
misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss 'the neural embedding baseline' as if it is a single agreed object.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of frozen penultimate-layer features from the pretrained ResNet-18 used in a prior internal report, with only the final head being trained in the current study.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the repository's current 'nn_embed' branch, a jointly trained shallow MLP embedding that feeds into the final classifier head.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both baselines are internally described as neural embeddings, both already exist in lab materials, and the shorthand sounds unambiguous to insiders who assume the same reference point.

misalignment_points.topic: How to match compute for random Fourier features
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'match compute' for the random Fourier feature approximation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes they will hold the random feature dimension fixed at a value like 4096 and reuse the same sampled Fourier map across seeds so that stochastic variation does not muddy the design review comparison.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes they will choose feature counts per method to keep wall-clock runtime roughly equal and will redraw the random Fourier map for each seed as part of normal experimental variance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both approaches are standard ways practitioners operationalize fairness, and 'match compute' sounds like a settled implementation detail rather than something that needs explicit unpacking in a high-level review.

The whole point is to extend the earlier NTK-style Gram-spectrum intuition into a deeper setting where the representation map is everything before the last hidden layer, then show that the induced embedding gives cleaner optimization behavior and decent IID test performance. If we start adding too many empirical branches, theory reviewers will say the causal story is blurry.
